title: Short Stuff: Liberty Bell
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Liberty Bell. The hosts open with banter about the band Ween, then trace the bell's history from its 1751 commissioning by the Pennsylvania Provincial Assembly as the State House Bell, cast by Lester and Pack in London. They cover the first crack in 1752, the replacement bell Lester and Pack supplied and the melting of the original, wartime removals in 1777, the 1824 Lafayette visit and renaming, abolitionist use of the bell, the second crack and its theories (1835 John Marshall death, Fourth of July, Washington's birthday), the high tin content theory from 1975 research, the failed 1846 stop-drilling repair, and the bell's role as a symbol on a World War I Liberty Bond tour. The episode ends with a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, with Jerry sitting in for Dave, and chat about the band Ween and a song about the Liberty Bell.

segments.title: Introduction and 1751 origins
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Liberty Bell as a fraud in name and go back to 1751, when the bell arrived at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia. It was originally just a working bell.

segments.title: Original bell and casting
segments.summary: The bell was commissioned as the State House Bell by the Pennsylvania Provincial Assembly and cast by Lester and Pack in London. It bore an inscription from Leviticus, was about three feet high, and weighed about 2,100 pounds.

segments.title: First crack and replacement
segments.summary: The original bell reportedly cracked the first time it was used in 1752. Lester and Pack supplied a replacement, and the Assembly let them keep the original to melt into a second bell.

segments.title: Two bells confusion
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the confusing situation of the replacement bell and the recast bell both existing in the State House, and which one is the official Liberty Bell.

segments.title: Wartime removal, 1824 renaming, and abolitionists
segments.summary: The bell was removed in 1777 during the British advance and rehung in 1785. Lafayette's 1824 visit and later renaming led to the name Liberty Bell, and abolitionists used it to speak against slavery.

segments.title: Second crack and its theories
segments.summary: The recast bell cracked, with the cause uncertain. Theories point to ringing for John Marshall's death in 1835, Fourth of July celebrations in the 1840s, or George Washington's birthday. The National Park Service says it cracked from age.

segments.title: High tin content research
segments.summary: Researchers in 1975 argued the bell was destined to crack because of its high tin content, which made it brittle for a bell meant to be rung.

segments.title: 1846 stop-drilling repair and retirement
segments.summary: In 1846, workers tried to repair the bell by stop drilling, which widened the crack to about 21 inches long. Another crack developed, and the bell was no longer rung.

segments.title: Symbol and World War I Liberty Bonds tour
segments.summary: The bell became a symbol and in World War I toured the United States by train to promote Liberty Bonds, raising billions in today's dollars. The hosts say about a quarter of the country saw it.

segments.title: Brief closing banter
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a sports email, and Josh moves to wrap up the episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes with the iHeartRadio production credit and directs listeners to the iHeartRadio app and other podcast platforms.
